sec.t:
जब [[magma|मैग्मा]] ज़मीन के बहुत नीचे धीरे-धीरे ठंडा होता है, तो क्रिस्टलों को बड़ा होने का समय मिलता है। कुछ ग्रेनाइट में तुम्हारे अँगूठे से भी बड़े क्रिस्टल होते हैं, और कुछ ठंडे होते मैग्मा पुखराज और टूरमलीन जैसे रत्न बनाते हैं।

पानी भी बहुत काम करता है। ज़मीन के बहुत नीचे का गर्म पानी घुले हुए खनिजों को दरारों और खोखली जगहों में ले जाता है। ठंडा होते-होते दीवारों पर क्रिस्टल जमते जाते हैं। बैंगनी नुकीले कटैला (एमेथिस्ट) से भरा खोखला पत्थर, जिसे जियोड कहते हैं, इसी तरह, परमाणुओं की एक-एक परत करके बना। पन्ना भी अक्सर ऐसी ही गर्म पानी वाली दरारों में उगता है।

लगभग दो हज़ार सालों तक भारत दुनिया में हीरों का मुख्य स्रोत रहा। बहुत-से मशहूर हीरे आज के [[@hyderabad|हैदराबाद]] के पास गोलकुंडा के आसपास के इलाके की नदी-बजरी से आए। व्यापारी इन्हें [[@ancient-persia|फ़ारस]], यूरोप और चीन तक ले गए। 1700 के दशक में ब्राज़ील में हीरे मिलने के बाद ही भारत की यह बढ़त ख़त्म हुई।

माना जाता है कि होप हीरा, लगभग 45 कैरेट का एक गहरा नीला पत्थर, इन्हीं भारतीय खदानों से आया। आज यह वॉशिंगटन डीसी में [[@smithsonian|स्मिथसोनियन]] के प्राकृतिक इतिहास संग्रहालय में रखा है, और किसी भी [[@museums|संग्रहालय]] में सबसे ज़्यादा देखी जाने वाली चीज़ों में से एक है। इसका नीलापन बोरॉन नाम के तत्व की ज़रा-सी मात्रा से आता है।

कोहिनूर, जिसके नाम का फ़ारसी में मतलब है "रोशनी का पहाड़", भी गोलकुंडा इलाके से आया माना जाता है। यह मुग़ल बादशाहों, फ़ारसी और अफ़ग़ान शासकों और सिख महाराजा रणजीत सिंह के हाथों से गुज़रा। 1849 में अंग्रेज़ इसे ले गए। अब यह [[@london-tower|टावर ऑफ़ लंदन]] में रखे ब्रिटिश राजमुकुट रत्नों का हिस्सा है, और भारत, पाकिस्तान और अफ़ग़ानिस्तान, तीनों ने इसे लौटाने की माँग की है।

1812 में फ़्रेडरिक मोह्स नाम के एक जर्मन वैज्ञानिक ने एक सीधा-सादा पैमाना बनाया। उन्होंने दस खनिजों को सबसे नरम से सबसे सख़्त तक इस हिसाब से रखा कि कौन किसे खरोंच सकता है। टैल्क 1 पर है, जिसे तुम नाख़ून से खरोंच सकते हो। क्वार्ट्ज़ 7 पर है। कोरंडम, माणिक और नीलम वाला खनिज, 9 पर है। हीरा 10 पर है।

सख़्ती ही वजह है कि रत्न टिके रहते हैं। हीरा काँच को आसानी से खरोंच देता है, और पहले लोग हीरों को इसी तरह परखते थे। पर हर रत्न क्रिस्टल नहीं होता। [[@pearls|मोती]] सीपियों के अंदर उगते हैं, और [[@amber-fossils|तृणमणि (एम्बर)]] पेड़ की सख़्त हुई राल है, फिर भी दोनों रत्नों में गिने जाते हैं।

text: टुंड्रा ठंडी, बिना पेड़ों वाली ज़मीन है। यह सुदूर उत्तर में, आर्कटिक महासागर के चारों ओर मिलती है, और दुनिया भर के पहाड़ों पर बहुत ऊँचाई पर भी, उस रेखा के ऊपर जहाँ पेड़ उगना बंद हो जाते हैं।

वहाँ सिर्फ़ नीचे-नीचे उगने वाले पौधे जी पाते हैं: काई, लाइकेन, घास, छोटी झाड़ियाँ और फूल, जो हवा से बचने के लिए ज़मीन से चिपके रहते हैं। टुंड्रा शब्द एक फ़िनिश और सामी शब्द से आया है, जिसका मतलब है बिना पेड़ों वाली ऊँची ज़मीन।

sec.t:
टुंड्रा की चाबी पर्माफ़्रॉस्ट है। गर्मियों में मिट्टी की बस ऊपरी परत पिघलती है, अक्सर एक मीटर से भी कम गहरी। उसके नीचे सब पत्थर की तरह जमा रहता है।

पिघली बर्फ़ नीचे बर्फ़ से होकर रिस नहीं पाती। इसलिए गर्मियों में टुंड्रा तालाबों, दलदलों और नालों का गीला-गीला पैबंद बन जाता है। हवाई जहाज़ से यह भूरे कालीन पर बिखरे टूटे काँच जैसा दिख सकता है।

पेड़ों की जड़ें जमी ज़मीन में नहीं धँस पातीं, और उगने का मौसम छोटा है, साल में लगभग 50 से 60 दिन। इसीलिए टुंड्रा के ज़्यादातर पौधे नन्हे हैं। आर्कटिक के कुछ विलो पेड़ पूरे बड़े हो चुके होते हैं, फिर भी ज़मीन से बस कुछ सेंटीमीटर ऊपर उठते हैं।

आर्कटिक में गर्मी आती है तो सूरज मुश्किल से डूबता है। पौधे कुछ ही हफ़्तों में उगने, फूलने और बीज बनाने की होड़ में लग जाते हैं।

दावत उड़ाने जानवर आ पहुँचते हैं। कैरिबू के विशाल झुंड, जिन्हें यूरोप और एशिया में रेनडियर कहते हैं, गर्मी के पौधे चरने सैकड़ों किलोमीटर पैदल चलते हैं। लाखों हंस, सैंडपाइपर और दूसरे पक्षी घोंसले बनाने उत्तर की ओर [[@migration|प्रवास]] करते हैं, क्योंकि यहाँ खाना भरपूर है और दक्षिण से कम [[predator|शिकारी]] हैं। तालाबों से मच्छर बादलों की तरह निकल पड़ते हैं।

कुछ जानवर साल भर यहीं रहते हैं। आर्कटिक लोमड़ी सर्दियों में सफ़ेद हो जाती है। मस्क ऑक्स के बाल इतने घने होते हैं कि ठंड मुश्किल से उनकी खाल तक पहुँचती है। लेमिंग बर्फ़ के नीचे सुरंगों में रहते हैं, जहाँ खुली हवा से ज़्यादा गर्मी होती है।

टुंड्रा देखने के लिए आर्कटिक जाना ज़रूरी नहीं। किसी भी पहाड़ पर काफ़ी ऊँचे चढ़ो, तो जंगल पतला होते-होते ख़त्म हो जाता है। पेड़ों की इस सीमा के ऊपर ऐल्पाइन टुंड्रा होता है।

भारत में ऐल्पाइन टुंड्रा ऊँचे हिमालय के हिस्सों में फैला है, जैसे [[@ladakh|लद्दाख]], स्पीति और उत्तरी सिक्किम में। यहाँ ज़मीन से गद्दी की तरह चिपके मज़बूत पौधे, याक, भरल और, बहुत कम ही सही, हिम तेंदुआ मिलता है। अमेरिका के रॉकी माउंटेन नेशनल पार्क में ऐसा टुंड्रा है, जहाँ तुम ट्रेल रिज रोड से गाड़ी चलाकर पहुँच सकते हो।

ऐल्पाइन टुंड्रा में आम तौर पर पर्माफ़्रॉस्ट नहीं होता, पर तेज़ हवाएँ, चुभती धूप और गर्मियों में भी ठंडी रातें होती हैं।

लोग हज़ारों साल से आर्कटिक के टुंड्रा पर रहते आए हैं। कनाडा, ग्रीनलैंड और [[@alaska|अलास्का]] के इनुइट लोग सील, व्हेल और कैरिबू का शिकार करते थे। उत्तरी यूरोप के सामी और साइबेरिया के नेनेत्स लोग सदियों से रेनडियर पालते आए हैं और उनके पीछे-पीछे पूरे इलाक़े में घूमते हैं।

अब उनकी ज़िंदगी बदल रही है। आर्कटिक धरती की लगभग किसी भी दूसरी जगह से तेज़ी से गर्म हो रहा है।

पर्माफ़्रॉस्ट एक विशाल फ़्रीज़र की तरह है। इसमें बहुत पहले मरे पौधों और जानवरों के अवशेष रखे हैं, जो कभी पूरी तरह सड़े ही नहीं। वैज्ञानिकों का अनुमान है कि दुनिया के पर्माफ़्रॉस्ट में आज की पूरी हवा से लगभग दोगुना कार्बन जमा है।

टुंड्रा गर्म होता है, तो ज़मीन की बर्फ़ पिघलती है। [[microbe|सूक्ष्मजीव]] जाग उठते हैं और पुराने अवशेषों को तोड़ने लगते हैं। वे कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड और मीथेन छोड़ते हैं। ये ऐसी [[greenhouse-gas|गैसें]] हैं जो और गर्मी रोकती हैं और [[@climate-change|जलवायु परिवर्तन]] को बढ़ाती हैं।

पिघलता पर्माफ़्रॉस्ट ऊपर भी मुसीबत खड़ी करता है। अलास्का और साइबेरिया के कुछ हिस्सों में सड़कें टेढ़ी-मेढ़ी हो जाती हैं, घर झुक जाते हैं और अंदर की बर्फ़ ग़ायब होते ही ज़मीन धँसकर गड्ढे बन जाती है।

text: Earth is round. Photos from space, ships sailing around it, and the curved shadow it casts on the Moon all prove it. But scientists enjoy asking "what if", because it shows how things really work.

If Earth were a flat disc, [[gravity|gravity]] would not pull straight down everywhere. It would pull towards the centre of the disc. Near the middle, things would feel normal. Near the edge, "down" would point sideways and inwards, so the ground would feel like a steep hill. Oceans and air would slide towards the centre. The rim would be a dry, airless, freezing wasteland.
And the strangest part? A flat Earth could not stay flat. Its own gravity would crush it back into a ball.

st.prompt: On a flat, disc-shaped Earth, where would most of the ocean water end up?

options.t: Piled up in the middle of the disc
Pouring off the edges like a waterfall
Spread evenly in a thin layer everywhere

st.reveal: Gravity pulls towards the centre of a planet's mass. On a disc, that is the middle, so water would flow inwards and form a huge dome-shaped sea there, leaving the outer rim dry.

sec.t:
[[@gravity-fall|Gravity]] pulls everything towards the centre of a planet's mass. On a ball, that is the middle of the ball, so "down" points straight under your feet wherever you stand.

On a disc, the [[centre-of-mass|centre of mass]] is in the middle of the flat face. Stand near the centre and gravity pulls straight down. Walk outwards and it starts to tug you back towards the middle as well. By the time you neared the rim, walking would feel like climbing a mountain thousands of kilometres long, even though the ground looked flat.

sec.h: Day and night all at once
sec.t:
On our round Earth, half the planet is in sunlight at any moment. That is why it is morning in Mumbai when it is night in New York. It is all about how a spinning ball meets the Sun, as explained in [[@day-night|day and night]].

On a flat disc facing the Sun, the whole side would get daylight at once. Sunrise would happen everywhere at the same time. Time zones would be pointless. When the disc turned edge-on, sunlight would hit only the rim, and then the far side would be in daylight while ours went dark.

Anything big enough gets squeezed into a ball by its own gravity. Every bit pulls on every other bit, so lumps get dragged down and dips filled in. The only shape where every part of the surface is equally close to the middle is a sphere.

For rocky worlds, this happens once they are very roughly 600 km across or bigger. Earth is about 12,700 km across, so it had no choice. Small [[asteroid|asteroids]] can stay lumpy like potatoes, because they are too small to crush themselves.

Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes in Egypt noticed that at noon on the longest day, the Sun shone straight down a well in the town of Syene. In Alexandria, further north, it cast a short shadow. Using the angle of that shadow and the distance between the towns, he worked out Earth's size. His answer was surprisingly close.

The Greek thinker Aristotle had pointed to the round shadow Earth throws on the Moon during a lunar [[eclipse|eclipse]]. In 499 CE, the Indian [[astronomer|astronomer]] [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]] wrote that Earth is round and spins, which is why the stars seem to move across the sky.

Sailors saw the proof too: a ship sailing away disappears hull first, then mast. On a flat sea it would simply shrink. And the most dramatic evidence turns up about once or twice a year, when Earth's curved shadow slides across the Moon during an [[@eclipses|eclipse]].

text: Start with your own eyes. Find a place away from bright lights, such as a rooftop, a garden or a field, and go with an adult. Switch off your phone screen and wait. It takes about 20 to 30 minutes for your eyes to fully adjust to the dark, and the longer you wait, the more stars appear.

Learn a few bright patterns first, like Orion in winter or the Saptarishi, which Americans call the Big Dipper. Use them as signposts to find other stars. A free sky map or app can help you name what you see.
Once you know your way around, a pair of [[@telescopes-make|binoculars]] will show you [[crater|craters]] on the Moon, the moons of Jupiter and clusters of stars invisible to the naked eye.

st.prompt: You spot a bright point of light that doesn't twinkle, while the stars around it do. What is it most likely to be?
st.reveal: Stars are so far away that they are tiny points, and moving air bends their light about, making them twinkle. Planets are much closer, so they appear as tiny discs. The wobbles average out, and they shine more steadily.

d.try: With an adult, go out on a clear night and roll a sheet of paper into a tube. Look through it at one patch of sky and count the stars you can see. Try it again on a different night, or from a darker place, and compare the numbers. Never look at the Sun, with or without the tube.
myth: The North Star is the brightest star in the sky.

Polaris is only moderately bright, around 48th in the list of brightest stars. It is famous because it sits almost exactly above Earth's North Pole, so it barely moves while other stars circle around it.

sec.t:
Your [[@eyes-see|eyes]] have two kinds of light-sensing cells. One kind sees colours and works in bright light. The other works in dim light but sees only shades of grey. When you step into the dark, the dim-light cells slowly become more sensitive.

A single glance at a bright phone screen resets them. That is why many stargazers use a torch covered in red cellophane. Red light disturbs night vision the least.

Here is a trick [[astronomer|astronomers]] use: to see a faint star, look slightly to one side of it. The edge of your vision is better at picking up dim light than the centre.

The sky looks like a jumble at first, but a few shapes help. In the winter months, Orion stands out, with three stars in a row for his belt. Follow the belt down to the left and you reach Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky.

In the northern sky, the seven stars of the Saptarishi, named after seven sages in Indian tradition, form a ladle shape. The two stars at the end of the bowl point to Polaris, the [[@north-star|North Star]]. In summer evenings, look south for Scorpius, with its red heart, Antares.

Planets wander slowly among the stars over weeks. They usually shine steadily instead of twinkling.

{{story:eyes-see}}

Not everything up there sits still. Watch for a bright, steady dot gliding across the sky with no flashing lights. It may be the [[@space-station|International Space Station]], which circles Earth about every 90 minutes. NASA's Spot the Station website tells you when it will pass over your town.

[[meteor|Meteor]] showers are great for beginners because you need no equipment at all. The Perseids peak around 12 August and the Geminids around 14 December. Lie back, look up and be patient. On a dark night, you might see dozens of [[@shooting-stars|shooting stars]] in an hour.

Light from streets, buildings and signs scatters in the air and drowns out faint stars. A 2016 study found that the Milky Way is hidden from more than a third of humanity, including about 80% of North Americans.

Some places are fighting back. In 2022, the area around the Indian Astronomical Observatory at Hanle, in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], was declared India's first dark sky reserve. Villagers there have been trained as astronomy guides, and homes use shielded lights that point downwards.

Every big step up in stargazing comes from collecting more light. Binoculars and telescopes use [[@lenses-glasses|lenses]] or mirrors to gather far more light than your eye can, showing things the ancient sky-watchers never saw. But the first step is the same as it was thousands of years ago: go outside and look up.

text: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef system on Earth. It lies in the warm, shallow sea off the coast of Queensland, in north-eastern [[@australia|Australia]]. It is not one long wall but about 2,900 separate reefs and hundreds of islands, stretching about 2,300 km. That is roughly the distance from Delhi to Kanyakumari.

It was built by corals, tiny animals called [[polyp|polyps]], each smaller than your fingernail. Each polyp builds a hard cup of limestone around its soft body. Over thousands of years, billions of these cups pile up into reefs. The reef is home to more than 1,500 kinds of fish, hundreds of kinds of coral, [[@sharks-myths|sharks]], rays, dolphins, whales, [[@sea-turtles|sea turtles]] and seabirds.

st.prompt: What gives living coral most of its colour?

options.t: Tiny algae living inside the coral animals
The colour of the rocks underneath

st.reveal: Most reef corals have tiny algae living inside their bodies. The algae make food from sunlight and share it with the coral, and they give it much of its colour. When the water gets too hot, the coral loses its algae and turns white.

It can't. Astronauts orbiting a few hundred kilometres up can see parts of the reef, but from the Moon, about 384,000 km away, no single structure on Earth is visible.

sec.t:
A coral polyp looks like a tiny tube with [[tentacle|tentacles]] around its mouth. At night, many polyps stretch out their tentacles to catch drifting food. But most of their food comes from somewhere surprising: tiny [[algae|algae]] living inside their bodies.

These algae use sunlight to make sugar, and they share it with the coral. In return, the coral gives them shelter. That is why reef-building corals need clear, sunny, shallow water. With this energy, the polyps slowly build their limestone skeletons. When polyps die, new ones grow on top. A large reef can be the work of thousands of years. Coral reefs in general are crowded with life, as you can read in [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]].

Corals are sensitive to heat. When the sea stays too warm for weeks, corals throw out their helpful algae. Without them, the coral turns white, which is called bleaching. Bleached coral is not dead yet, but if the heat goes on too long, it starves.

The Great Barrier Reef suffered mass bleaching in 1998 and 2002, and again in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025. Scientists link these events to warming seas caused by [[@climate-change|climate change]]. Some areas have recovered well between events, but the gaps between them are getting shorter. Outbreaks of the crown-of-thorns [[@starfish|starfish]], which eats coral, add to the damage.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived beside the reef and fished its waters for tens of thousands of years. Their stories and knowledge of the sea are much older than any map. In 1770, the British explorer James Cook's ship, the Endeavour, ran aground on the reef and had to be repaired on the shore.

The reef became a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site in 1981, and most of it is protected as a [[@marine-parks-india|marine park]]. India has coral reefs too, though much smaller: in the Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kutch, [[@lakshadweep|Lakshadweep]] and around the [[@andaman|Andaman and Nicobar Islands]]. The USA has reefs off Florida and Hawaii. All of them face the same rising heat.

text: The sea is rising for two main reasons, both caused by a warming [[climate|climate]]. First, the oceans are getting warmer, and warm water takes up a little more space than cold water. Second, ice on land is melting. Mountain [[@glaciers|glaciers]] and the huge [[@what-if-ice-melted|ice sheets]] of Greenland and Antarctica are losing ice, and the meltwater runs into the sea.

Since 1880, the average sea level around the world has risen by more than 20 cm. Most of that rise has happened in the last few decades, and it is getting faster. Today the sea is rising by about 4 mm a year. That sounds tiny, but over a lifetime it adds up, and higher seas let storms and high tides push farther inland. Scientists link the warming to [[@climate-change|climate change]] caused mostly by burning coal, oil and gas.

st.prompt: Why does warmer seawater make the sea level rise, even without any ice melting?

options.t: Water takes up more space as it warms
Fish grow bigger in warm water

st.reveal: Like most things, water expands slightly when it warms. A tiny expansion in a deep ocean adds up to a lot. For much of the last century, this expansion caused a large part of the rise. Today, melting land ice adds even more.

Then place ice cubes on a small upturned cup inside a bowl of water, so they sit above the water, and mark the level. Which one raises the water when it melts?
myth: Melting sea ice in the Arctic is the main reason the sea is rising.

Sea ice already floats, so when it melts it hardly changes the sea level, just like ice in a glass. The rise comes from ice melting on land, in glaciers and ice sheets, and from warming water expanding.

sec.t:
Almost everything expands when it warms. Railway tracks have small gaps so they don't buckle on hot days. Water does the same. The ocean has soaked up most of the extra heat trapped by [[greenhouse-gas|greenhouse gases]], and as it warms, it swells.

Each bit of water expands only a little. But the ocean is very deep, so a tiny stretch in every metre adds up. Between 1971 and 2018, this expansion caused about half of the sea level rise, according to the IPCC, the world's main panel of climate scientists. In recent years, melting land ice has become the bigger part.

sec.h: Ice on land and ice at sea

sec.t:
Sea level goes up and down every day with the [[@tides|tides]], and waves make it bumpy. So how do scientists measure such a small change? For more than a century, tide gauges at harbours have recorded the height of the water every few minutes. Averaging over years cancels out the tides and waves.

Since 1992, [[@satellites-help|satellites]] have measured the height of the sea from space. They bounce radar pulses off the water and time how long the echo takes. Together, gauges and satellites show the rise clearly. They also show that it is not the same everywhere. In some places, such as Jakarta in Indonesia, [[@earth-sinking-cities|the land itself is sinking]], which makes the sea seem to rise even faster.

Low-lying places feel rising seas first. Some islands in the Indian Sundarbans have been shrinking, partly because of rising water and [[erosion|erosion]], and people have had to move. That area is also home to tigers and [[@mangroves|mangroves]], as you can read in [[@sundarbans-tigers|Sundarbans tigers]]. The [[@maldives|Maldives]], most of which lies less than 1 m above sea level, is planning for the future, and so are cities like [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], Kolkata, [[@miami|Miami]] and New York.

Scientists expect the sea to rise somewhere between about 30 cm and 1 m more by 2100, depending on how much the world cuts its emissions. Coastal cities are building sea walls, raising roads and restoring mangroves and [[@wetlands|wetlands]] that soak up storm surges.

text: The animal with the longest life we can actually count is a clam. An ocean quahog, pulled up from the seabed off Iceland in 2006, had 507 growth lines in its shell, one for each year. Among animals with a backbone, the record probably belongs to the Greenland shark. A 2016 study found the largest ones are at least 272 years old, and most likely about 400.
On land, the champion is a giant tortoise named Jonathan, who lives on the island of St Helena in the Atlantic. He hatched around 1832 and was about 194 in 2026, still munching grass.

st.prompt: How did scientists work out the age of Greenland sharks, which have no growth rings in their bones?

By counting rings on their teeth
By measuring how long their fins were

st.reveal: The centre of a shark's eye lens forms before birth and never changes. Scientists measured a form of carbon in it, a bit like the method used to date ancient bones, and found the biggest shark was probably around 400 years old.

d.try: Make a "lifespan ladder". On a long strip of paper, mark one centimetre for every year. Put a mouse at 2 cm, a dog at about 12 cm, a human at about 80 cm, a bowhead whale at 2 m and a Greenland shark at about 4 m. Unroll it down a corridor and stand at each mark.
myth: Bigger animals always live longer than smaller ones.
Size helps, but it's far from the whole story. A naked mole rat the size of a sausage can live over 35 years, ten times longer than a rat. Cold, slow lives often matter more than size.

sec.t:
Greenland sharks live in freezing water, mostly in the North Atlantic and Arctic. They grow about one centimetre a year and swim so slowly they look half asleep. The study suggested females don't have babies until they are around 150 years old.

Because they have no bony rings to count, scientists looked inside their eyes. The middle of the eye lens forms before birth and never changes. Measuring carbon in it gave the age. The biggest shark tested, about 5 metres long, came out at somewhere between 272 and 512 years, with about 400 as the best guess.

sec.h: Whales, tortoises and a clam named Ming
sec.t:
Bowhead whales, which live in the Arctic, can pass 200. Hunters in Alaska have found old stone and ivory harpoon tips buried in living whales, made in styles that were last used over a hundred years earlier.

[[@turtles-tortoises|Tortoises]] are famous for long lives too. Kolkata's Alipore Zoo once had an Aldabra giant tortoise called Adwaita, who died in 2006. Some claimed he was 250, though nobody could prove it.

The 507-year-old clam was nicknamed Ming, after the Chinese [[dynasty|dynasty]] that ruled when it was young. Sadly, scientists only learned its age after opening it.

{{story:trees-oldest}}

Many record holders share a pattern: they live in cold places, move slowly and grow slowly. A slow body burns energy gently and may build up damage more slowly. Some, like tortoises and clams, are also well protected from [[predator|predators]], so they have time to grow old.

The [[@power-naked-mole-rat|naked mole rat]] breaks the rules. It's a small, wrinkly rodent from East Africa that can live more than 35 years, while ordinary rats manage about three. Scientists study it closely, hoping to learn more about [[@ageing|ageing]] in people.

sec.h: How long do pets and people live?
sec.t:
For comparison, most dogs live about 10 to 13 years and cats around 12 to 18. A mouse is old at two. Elephants can reach 60 or 70, and a few famous parrots have lived past 80, outliving their first owners.

People are long-lived for [[mammal|mammals]] of our size. The oldest person whose age was carefully checked was Jeanne Calment of France, who died in 1997 aged 122 years and 164 days. She was born in 1875 and said she had met the painter Vincent van Gogh as a girl.

Plants beat every animal. Some bristlecone pines in California are more than 4,800 years old. Certain aspen groves and seagrass meadows grow as giant connected clones, and they may be older still.

Some animals blur the idea of age altogether. Glass sponges on the deep seabed may live for thousands of years, though their ages are hard to check. Tiny freshwater animals called hydras keep replacing their cells and show almost no signs of getting old.

And the strangest part? A small jellyfish in the Mediterranean can turn itself back into a baby when it's hurt or starving, which is why some call it [[@jellyfish-old|the immortal jellyfish]].

text: A glow stick is a plastic tube holding two separate liquids. One liquid sits inside a thin glass tube, and the other fills the space around it. When you bend the stick, the glass cracks and the two liquids mix.

That mix starts a chemical reaction that gives off energy. A colourful dye in the liquid catches that energy and lets it out again as light. Because almost none of the energy becomes heat, a glow stick stays cool in your hand. Scientists call this *chemiluminescence*, which simply means light from chemistry.

st.prompt: You drop one glow stick into a cup of warm water and another into a cup of ice water. What happens?

options.t: The warm one glows brighter but runs out sooner

st.reveal: Heat makes molecules move faster and bump into each other more often, so the reaction speeds up. The glow gets brighter, but the chemicals get used up sooner. Cold does the opposite.

sec.t:
A traditional light bulb works by heating a wire until it glows white hot. Most of the electricity becomes heat, which is why old bulbs could burn your fingers. A candle wastes even more energy as heat.

A glow stick skips the heat. The energy from the reaction goes almost straight into light. That makes it safe to use where a spark could be dangerous, such as near leaking gas or fuel. Soldiers, divers, miners and rescue teams carry them because they work in rain and under water and cannot set anything on fire.

sec.h: Speed it up, slow it down
sec.t:
Like most chemical reactions, the glow stick reaction runs faster when it is warm. Drop a glowing stick into warm water and it becomes much brighter, but it may fade within an hour or two. Put it in a freezer and it dims to a faint shine, yet it can keep going for a day or more.

This is why people sometimes save half-used glow sticks in the freezer. It works, but it is not a recharge. The chemicals are simply being used more slowly. Once they run out, the stick is finished.

In the early 1960s, chemists in the USA, including Edwin Chandross at Bell Laboratories, studied reactions that gave off light. Researchers at a company called American Cyanamid then found brighter and longer-lasting mixtures. The US Navy was interested, because sailors needed a light that would not spark.

By the 1970s, glow sticks were sold in shops. Since then they have been used as safety lights, fishing lures, Halloween costumes and concert decorations. Inside, they should never be cut open, because the liquid can sting skin and eyes.

People did not invent cold light, though. Living things got there first, hundreds of millions of years earlier. [[@fireflies|Fireflies]] flash to find mates, using a reaction that turns almost all its energy into light. Glowing mushrooms, squid and jellyfish do the same. And in the black depths of the sea, the [[@anglerfish|anglerfish]] dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth, a living glow stick with teeth behind it. It is one of thousands of animals that glow in the dark ocean, a trick called [[@bioluminescence|bioluminescence]].

text: Speed cameras measure how fast a car is moving, then take a photo of its number plate if it is going too fast. They do this in a few different ways.

Some send out [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] and listen to the echo. Some fire quick pulses of laser light. Some use [[sensor|sensors]] buried in the road. Others photograph a car at two points far apart and time how long it took to travel between them.

The fastest of these measurements take less than a second. The camera then records the plate, the time, the place and the speed. In many countries, including India, a fine can then be sent straight to the owner's phone.

st.prompt: An average-speed camera sees a car at two points 10 km apart. The car takes 5 minutes. How fast was it going on average?
st.reveal: Five minutes is one-twelfth of an hour. Going 10 km in one-twelfth of an hour means 10 × 12 = 120 km in an hour. Average-speed cameras do this sum automatically.

sec.t:
Listen to an ambulance siren as it races past. As it comes towards you the sound is higher. As it moves away, it drops lower. That change is called the Doppler effect, after the Austrian scientist Christian Doppler, who described it in 1842.

Radio waves do the same thing. A radar speed camera sends out a beam of radio waves. When they hit a moving car, they bounce back slightly squashed if it's coming closer, or slightly stretched if it's going away. The camera's computer measures exactly how much the waves have changed. From that, it works out the car's speed.

Radar uses the same idea as the giant dishes that track aircraft and storms. Here it is shrunk into a box on a pole.

Some cameras don't measure speed by themselves at all. Instead, two sensors are set into the road a few metres apart. They might be loops of wire that notice the metal of a car passing over them, or strips that feel the pressure of tyres.

The system times how long the car takes to go from one sensor to the next. If the gap is 3 metres and the car crosses it in a tenth of a second, it is going 30 metres a second. That is 108 km/h. This is [[@speed-distance|speed and distance]] maths, done in an instant.

Some drivers slow down just before a camera, then speed up again. Average-speed cameras stop that trick. One camera reads a car's number plate. Another camera, perhaps many kilometres further on, reads it again. A computer divides the distance by the time taken.

If the average comes out too high, the car must have broken the limit somewhere in between. Cameras that read number plates are also used at toll plazas and in cities to spot stolen vehicles. The tag-reading system in [[@fastag-tolls|FASTag tolls]] is a close cousin.

In the 1950s, Maurice Gatsonides was a Dutch rally driver. He wanted to know how fast he took corners, so he helped design a device to measure speed. His company, Gatso, was founded in 1958 and went on to make speed cameras used in many countries.

There is some irony in that. A man who loved driving fast ended up giving police one of their best tools against speeding. And the strangest part? Some police radar guns can track several cars at once, using the same wave tricks that let scientists measure how fast distant [[galaxy|galaxies]] are rushing away.

यह नाम *लीपण* से आया है, जिसका मतलब है लिपाई। यह गाँव के घरों की अंदरूनी दीवारों की सजावट के रूप में शुरू हुआ, खास तौर पर भुंगा कहलाने वाली गोल झोपड़ियों में। आज यह उतनी ही आसानी से मुंबई, बेंगलुरु या न्यू जर्सी के किसी फ़्लैट में टँगे रंगे हुए लकड़ी के तख़्ते पर भी दिख जाता है।

sec.t:
पारंपरिक नुस्खा अजीब लगता है। औरतें स्थानीय मिट्टी में ऊँट या गधे की लीद मिलातीं, उसे गूँधकर चिकना करतीं और हाथ से बत्तियाँ बेलतीं। लीद के रेशे मिट्टी को बाँधे रखते हैं, इसलिए कच्छ की तेज़ धूप में सूखते समय वह कम चटकती है। रेगिस्तान में [[@camels|ऊँट]] हर जगह थे, इसलिए उनकी लीद आसानी से मिल जाती थी।

सूखने पर मिट्टी पर सफ़ेद मिट्टी का घोल पोता जाता। शीशे, जिन्हें *आभला* कहते हैं, नन्हे गोलों, त्रिकोणों और हीरों में काटे जाते। कुछ तो मुश्किल से नाखून जितने बड़े होते। एक बड़ी दीवार पर सैकड़ों शीशे हो सकते थे, और हर एक मिट्टी के गीले रहते हाथ से जड़ा जाता।

कच्छ के अलग-अलग समुदायों की अपनी-अपनी शैलियाँ हैं। रबारी औरतें, जो सदियों से ऊँट, भेड़ और बकरियाँ चराने वाले पशुपालक समुदाय से हैं, ऐसे नमूनों के लिए जानी जाती हैं जिनमें उनकी [[embroidery|कढ़ाई]] की झलक मिलती है। बन्नी के घास के मैदानों के मुतवा लोगों में मर्द भी लिप्पन बनाते थे। मेघवाल कारीगरों के भी अपने डिज़ाइन हैं।

नमूने ज़्यादातर [[geometry|ज्यामितीय]] होते हैं, जो किसी केंद्र के चारों ओर दोहराए गए आकारों से बनते हैं। इसीलिए लिप्पन की [[@rangoli-symmetry|रंगोली]] से, और कच्छ की मशहूर शीशे वाली कढ़ाई से, खूब मिलती-जुलती है। किसी रबारी औरत के घाघरे और उसकी दीवार पर एक ही डिज़ाइन हो सकता था।

sec.h: गाँव की दीवारों से शहर के फ़्लैटों तक
sec.t:
पिछले 20 सालों में लिप्पन गाँव से बाहर निकल आया है। कलाकार अब लीद की जगह क्राफ़्ट मिट्टी या पुट्टी इस्तेमाल करते हैं, और उसे दीवारों की जगह लकड़ी के तख़्तों पर चिपकाते हैं। शीशे पहले से कटे आते हैं। ऑनलाइन किट बिकती हैं, और शहर के बच्चे स्कूल की कला कक्षाओं में लिप्पन बनाते हैं।

कुछ पारंपरिक कलाकारों को फ़िक्र है कि ये छोटे रास्ते असली लिप्पन का हुनर खो देते हैं, जिसमें हर बत्ती हाथ से बेली जाती है। दूसरे खुश हैं कि यह कला कारीगरों को रोज़ी दे रही है और नए घरों तक पहुँच रही है। कच्छ आने वाले सैलानी भी मदद करते हैं, खास तौर पर [[@gujarat-rann|कच्छ के रण]] के सफ़ेद नमक वाले रेगिस्तान में सर्दियों के उत्सव के दौरान।

कच्छ और राजस्थान में शीशे के काम की जड़ें गहरी हैं, कपड़ों में भी और दीवारों पर भी। बहुत-से लोग मानते हैं कि रोशनी की चमक बुरी नज़र को लौटा देती है। कुछ लोगों को भूरे और सफ़ेद रेगिस्तानी नज़ारे में बस चमक-दमक अच्छी लगती है। वजह जो भी हो, कच्छ ने चमकीले काँच को भारत की सबसे पहचानी जाने वाली दस्तकारियों में बदल दिया है, और लिप्पन के तख़्ते अब हवाई अड्डों और होटलों की लॉबी में टँगे हैं।

और इस इलाके के पास ऐसी और भी बहुत-सी चीज़ें हैं: ठप्पे की छपाई, बाँधकर रँगाई और चमड़े का काम, सब [[@india-wonder-kutch-crafts|कच्छ की दस्तकारियों]] की कहानी का हिस्सा।

text: फ़्रीडा काहलो (1907–1954) एक मेक्सिकन चित्रकार थीं, जो अपने चटख रंगों वाले आत्म-चित्रों के लिए सबसे ज़्यादा जानी जाती हैं। उन्होंने अपना चेहरा बार-बार पेंट किया, जुड़ी हुई गहरी भौंहें, बालों में फूल और रंग-बिरंगे पारंपरिक मेक्सिकन कपड़े। अपने चारों ओर उन्होंने बंदर, तोते, पौधे और मेक्सिको के इतिहास और लोक कला के प्रतीक बनाए।

उनकी ज़िंदगी दर्द से भरी थी। बचपन की बीमारी और एक भयानक हादसे ने उन्हें ज़िंदगी भर की चोटें दीं, और उनके बहुत-से ऑपरेशन हुए। उन्होंने इन अनुभवों को ऐसी पेंटिंग में बदल दिया जो एक साथ ईमानदार, अजीब और चमकदार हैं। अपने समय में मेक्सिको के बाहर वे बहुत मशहूर नहीं थीं, पर आज वे दुनिया की सबसे पहचानी जाने वाली कलाकारों में से एक हैं।

फ़्रीडा का जन्म कोयोआकान में हुआ, जो उस समय मेक्सिको सिटी के किनारे बसा एक शांत कस्बा था, एक ऐसे घर में जिसे उनके परिवार ने चटख नीले रंग से रँगा था। लगभग छह साल की उम्र में उन्हें [[@polio-india|पोलियो]] हो गया, एक ऐसी बीमारी जो [[@muscles|पेशियों]] को नुकसान पहुँचा सकती है। इससे उनका दायाँ पैर बाएँ से पतला और कमज़ोर रह गया, और बाद में वे कुछ हद तक इसे छिपाने के लिए लंबी स्कर्ट पहनने लगीं।

1925 में, 18 साल की उम्र में, वे स्कूल से घर लौट रही थीं जब उनकी बस एक ट्राम से टकरा गई। उनकी रीढ़, कूल्हे की हड्डी और एक पैर बुरी तरह टूट गए। वे महीनों तक प्लास्टर में सीधी लेटी रहीं।

1929 में फ़्रीडा ने डिएगो रिवेरा से शादी की, जो तब तक मेक्सिको के सबसे मशहूर चित्रकार थे। वे सार्वजनिक दीवारों पर मज़दूरों, किसानों और मेक्सिको के इतिहास को दिखाने वाले विशाल [[mural|भित्ति-चित्रों]] के लिए जाने जाते थे। उनकी शादी उथल-पुथल भरी थी। वे अलग हुए, 1939 में तलाक़ हुआ और अगले साल फिर से शादी कर ली।

दोनों साथ में अमेरिका गए, जहाँ डिएगो ने [[@san-francisco|सैन फ़्रांसिस्को]], डेट्रॉइट और न्यूयॉर्क में भित्ति-चित्र बनाए। फ़्रीडा को वहाँ घर की याद सताती थी, और उन्होंने ख़ुद को व्यस्त अमेरिकी फ़ैक्टरियों और मेक्सिको की प्राचीन दुनिया के बीच खड़ा हुआ पेंट किया।

फ़्रीडा को मेक्सिको का अतीत बहुत प्यारा था, जिसमें [[@aztecs-maya|एज़्टेक और माया]] [[civilisation|सभ्यताएँ]] भी शामिल थीं, और उसकी जीती-जागती परंपराएँ भी। वे अक्सर दक्षिणी मेक्सिको की तेहुआना औरतों की लंबी, [[embroidery|कढ़ाई]] वाली स्कर्ट और ब्लाउज़ पहनती थीं। उन्होंने *रेताब्लो* कहलाने वाली छोटी मेक्सिकन लोक पेंटिंग की शैली में चित्र बनाए, जिन्हें आम लोग किसी हादसे या बीमारी से बच निकलने पर धन्यवाद देने के लिए बनवाते थे, कुछ-कुछ हमारे यहाँ मन्नत पूरी होने पर चढ़ाई जाने वाली चीज़ों की तरह।

1939 में [[@paris|पेरिस]] में उनकी प्रदर्शनी लगी। लूव्र ने उनकी एक कृति, *द फ़्रेम*, ख़रीदी, जो चित्रित चिड़ियों और फूलों से घिरा एक छोटा आत्म-चित्र है। वहाँ के मशहूर कलाकारों ने उनकी तारीफ़ की, हालाँकि फ़्रीडा को पेरिस की कला की दुनिया कुछ ख़ास पसंद नहीं आई।

आख़िरी बरसों में फ़्रीडा की सेहत और बिगड़ गई, और डॉक्टरों को उनके दाएँ पैर का एक हिस्सा काटना पड़ा। 1953 में मेक्सिको में उनकी पहली एकल प्रदर्शनी लगी। चलने लायक न होने के कारण वे एम्बुलेंस से पहुँचीं और उन्हें उनके अपने बिस्तर पर उठाकर अंदर लाया गया।

अगले साल 47 की उम्र में उसी नीले घर में उनकी मौत हुई जहाँ वे जन्मी थीं। आज वह फ़्रीडा काहलो संग्रहालय है, जहाँ दुनिया भर से लोग आते हैं। बहुत-से लोग, ख़ासकर बीमारी या विकलांगता के साथ जीने वाले, उन्हें ऐसी इंसान के रूप में देखते हैं जिसने उस चीज़ को छिपाने से इनकार कर दिया जो उन्हें दूसरों से अलग बनाती थी।

text: Cities keep growing because they pull people in. They offer more jobs, better schools and colleges, bigger hospitals and more ways to earn a living than most villages. When a factory, port or office opens, workers arrive. Then shops, schools and restaurants open to serve them, which brings more workers still.

Cities also grow from within, as children are born there, and outwards, as they spread and swallow nearby villages. Around 2007, more than half the world's people were living in towns and cities for the first time. The UN expects about two in three people to be city dwellers by 2050.

Migration from villages is important, but a large share of city growth comes from children born in cities and from villages near the edge being reclassified as towns as the city spreads.

sec.t:
Most people move to cities for work. A factory job, a construction site, a shop or an office can pay more than farming a small plot, especially in years when the rains fail. Cities also offer things that are hard to find in a village: colleges, specialist doctors, cinemas and a wide choice of friends.

Being close together helps businesses too. A company in [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]] can find skilled engineers nearby, along with suppliers, banks and customers. Economists call this the benefit of clustering. It is a big reason why cities that are already large keep getting larger.

The first cities appeared more than 5,000 years ago in [[@harappan-trade|Mesopotamia]], Egypt and the Indus Valley, after farmers began growing more food than they needed. Extra food meant some people could become potters, priests, traders or rulers instead.

Cities grew fastest during the [[@industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]] of the 1800s, when factories needed huge numbers of workers. [[@chicago|Chicago]] is a famous example. It had about 4,000 people in 1837. Railways, meat-packing plants and grain markets drew workers from across America and Europe, and by 1890 the city had more than a million people.

sec.h: Growing up as well as out
sec.t:
When land runs short, cities build upwards. Tall buildings let thousands of people live and work on one small plot. The first [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]] rose in Chicago and New York in the late 1800s, after steel frames and safe elevators were invented.

{{story:skyscrapers}}

About 31% of Indians lived in towns and cities at the 2011 [[census|census]], and the share has grown since. Delhi and [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] are among the largest urban areas anywhere, each with more than 2 crore people. Mumbai began as seven separate islands, joined over two centuries by land reclaimed from the sea.

Many people arrive in Indian cities faster than homes, water pipes and buses can be built. So some live in crowded informal settlements, such as [[@slums-housing|Dharavi]] in Mumbai, which is also home to thousands of small businesses making leather goods, pottery and recycled plastic.

In 1950, New York and [[@tokyo|Tokyo]] were the only urban areas in the world with more than 1 crore people. Today there are dozens of these "megacities", and many are in Asia, Africa and Latin America, including Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, [[@nigeria|Lagos]] and São Paulo.

Fast growth brings traffic jams, [[@air-pollution|air pollution]], flooding when drains cannot cope, and high rents. Cities around the world are trying to solve these with metro railways, better planning and more parks. Still, cities use land efficiently. Packing people together leaves more countryside free for farms and forests. Whether a city feels crowded or comfortable depends a lot on how well it is planned, and the world's [[@population|population]] means the choices made now will shape life for billions.

text: Kids almost everywhere help at home, but the jobs change a lot from place to place. In India, children often help set out water, fold clothes, shell peas or prepare the house for a festival. In the United States, many kids load dishwashers, take out rubbish bins and feed pets, sometimes for pocket money.
In Japan, children clean their own schools every day. In farming villages across Africa, Asia and Latin America, children may help care for younger siblings, fetch water or look after animals.
What counts as a normal chore depends on the family, the place and the age of the child. But the urge to help seems to start very young.

sec.t:
In many Japanese schools there is a daily time called o-soji, meaning cleaning. Pupils grab brooms, cloths and buckets. They sweep classrooms, mop corridors, wipe windows and clean the stairs. In some schools they clean the toilets too. Teachers often work alongside them.

The idea is that if you clean a place yourself, you are less likely to make a mess of it. Many Japanese schools also have pupils serve lunch to their classmates, wearing white caps and aprons.

Japanese children are also known for running errands young. A television show called "Hajimete no Otsukai", meaning "My First Errand", has shown toddlers going to shops alone since 1991. A camera crew follows them secretly. In 2022 it reached viewers worldwide on Netflix as "Old Enough!" You can see more everyday life in [[@japan-culture|Japan's culture]].

{{story:washing-machines}}

In 2006, two scientists in Germany, Felix Warneken and Michael Tomasello, ran a famous experiment. An adult "accidentally" dropped a pen or struggled to open a cupboard while carrying books. Toddlers just 18 months old would stop playing, toddle over and help. No one asked them, and no one rewarded them.

Psychologist Barbara Rogoff has studied children in Maya communities in Guatemala and Mexico. There, she found, children are often expected to join in family work from an early age, learning by watching and pitching in. Many of them help without being told, because they see themselves as part of the team.

Some researchers think that paying children for every small job can change how they feel about helping. Others think pocket money teaches useful lessons about earning and saving. Families decide differently, and there is no single right answer, as you can read in [[@money-pocket|the pocket money debate]].

Festivals bring extra jobs everywhere. Before Diwali, many Indian families clean and paint their homes, and children help draw rangoli patterns at the door. Before Lunar New Year in China, families sweep away the old year's dust. In the US, kids may help rake autumn leaves, or bake and decorate for Thanksgiving or Christmas.

These chores feel different from ordinary ones. They are tied to celebration, and many people remember them fondly for life.

Small jobs at home are part of family life. But some children around the world do heavy, dangerous work for long hours instead of going to school. That is [[@child-labour|child labour]], and it is very different. UNICEF and the International Labour Organization estimated that about 138 million children were in child labour worldwide in 2024, down from 160 million in 2020.

Chores are safe, short and suited to a child's age. They leave time for school, rest and play, which every child has a right to. School matters a great deal, and you can see how it works for children elsewhere in [[@schools-world|schools around the world]].

And the strangest part? The washing that took grandmothers all day can now take a machine an hour, and the clever spinning inside it is explained in [[@washing-machines|how washing machines work]].

text: Philosophy is thinking hard about big questions that can't be settled just by measuring or looking things up. What makes something fair? How do you know you aren't dreaming right now? Is it ever right to break a promise? Do animals have minds?

Scientists mostly ask what happens. Philosophers often ask what something means, and how we can know it. They answer with careful reasons, and they argue with each other to see which reasons hold up. Children are often very good at this, because they haven't yet learned to stop asking "but why?"

myth: Philosophy is just people sharing opinions, so any answer is as good as another.

Philosophers have to give reasons, and others test those reasons. Some arguments fall apart when you look closely, while others hold up. Logic, ethics and even science grew out of this careful checking.

sec.t:
Philosophers sort their questions into groups. **Ethics** asks how we should live and treat others, and books on [[ethics|ethics]] fill whole libraries. **Logic** studies what makes an argument strong or weak, and it later helped build [[@logic|logic]] for computers. A third group asks about **knowledge**: how do you know anything for certain? A fourth asks **what is real**: are numbers real things, or just ideas in our heads?

These questions sound abstract, but they turn up in daily life. When a cricket umpire decides whether a catch was clean, or a judge decides whether a law is fair, they are using ideas that philosophers argued about first.

In Greece, [[@socrates|Socrates]] walked the streets of Athens asking people questions until they realised they knew less than they thought. In China, [[@confucius|Confucius]] taught about kindness, family and good government. In India, the [[@buddha|Buddha]] asked why people suffer, and thinkers in schools such as Nyaya wrote detailed rules for reasoning and debate.

India had six classic schools of philosophy, called darshanas, as well as Buddhist and Jain thinkers and the Charvakas, who doubted anything they couldn't see. They argued with each other for centuries, and each side sharpened its ideas against the others.

In the 1970s, an American professor named Matthew Lipman noticed that his university students struggled to reason clearly. He decided it would help to start younger. He wrote stories for children that raised puzzles and let classes discuss them. His idea, called Philosophy for Children, has spread to schools in many countries.

Today the old questions are getting new life. Engineers building self-driving cars have to decide what the car should do in an emergency. People designing [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] argue about whether a machine could ever understand anything. Those are philosophy questions, and nobody has settled them yet.

You don't need a degree to start. Philosophy begins whenever someone asks a question and refuses to accept the first easy answer. Is it fair that the oldest child gets the biggest room? Should a robot pet have feelings? If everyone in your class lied once, would lying become all right?

Good philosophers listen as much as they talk. They try to say exactly what they mean, look for examples that might prove them wrong, and change their minds when a better reason comes along. It can feel strange at first to argue about something with no answer at the back of the book. That strangeness is a sign you've found a real philosophical question.

text: Pixar makes films by building whole worlds inside computers. Artists first design characters and sets on paper. Then modellers build them as 3D shapes on screen, and animators move them pose by pose, like puppets with thousands of strings. Finally, powerful computers work out how light falls on every surface and turn each moment into an image.

A film has 24 images, or frames, for every second. A 90-minute film needs about 130,000 frames. Each one is calculated by computers, and complex frames can take hours. Before any of that, though, a Pixar film spends years on its story.

st.reveal: Pixar animators set a character's key poses by hand on the computer, a bit like moving a very detailed puppet. The computer fills in the in-between frames, and the animators adjust them until the movement feels alive.

Computers do the heavy maths of drawing and lighting each frame, but people design every character, write the story, and decide every movement. A Pixar film takes hundreds of artists and engineers several years.

sec.h: Born in a Star Wars company
sec.t:
In the late 1970s, the film-maker George Lucas set up a computer graphics team inside his company, Lucasfilm. In 1986, Steve Jobs, a co-founder of Apple, bought that team, and it became Pixar.

That year, Pixar made a short film called Luxo Jr., about two desk lamps playing with a ball. The little lamp became the company's mascot and still hops across the screen at the start of every Pixar film.

In 1995, Pixar released Toy Story, the first feature film made entirely with [[@computers-how|computer]] animation. Disney, which had worked with Pixar on its films, bought the company in 2006.

Pixar's films start as ideas pitched by its directors. A small team writes and draws the story as thousands of sketches called storyboards. These are filmed in order with rough voices, making a crude version of the film called a story reel.

Directors then show these reels to a group of the studio's senior film-makers, who give honest notes on what isn't working. Pixar's co-founder Ed Catmull called this group the Braintrust. Films are often rebuilt many times. Inside Out, about the [[@emotions|emotions]] inside a girl's head, went through years of changes before its release in 2015.

Once the story works, modellers build every character and object as a 3D shape made of thousands of tiny flat surfaces. Riggers add hidden "bones" and controls, so animators can bend an elbow or lift an eyebrow.

Animators then pose the characters for each shot. Studying real movement is part of the job. For Finding Nemo, the team learned how fish swim and how light ripples under water.

Other teams handle things that are hard to animate by hand, like hair, cloth, water and crowds. In Monsters, Inc. (2001), the furry monster Sulley had more than 2 million individual hairs, each moving on its own.

Pixar's films travel widely, from a Mexican boy who loves music in Coco to a Chinese-Canadian girl in Turning Red. In 2015, Pixar released Sanjay's Super Team, a short film by the animator Sanjay Patel. It was based on his own childhood: a boy bored by his father's prayers who imagines Hindu gods as superheroes. It was nominated for an Oscar.

text: Kho-kho is a chasing game from Maharashtra, played by millions of Indian children. Until recently, few people outside South Asia had heard of it. That has changed fast.

In January 2025, New Delhi hosted the first Kho Kho World Cup. Men's and women's teams came from 23 countries, including Nepal, Iran, Kenya, South Africa, Brazil, the United States, England and Australia. India won both titles, beating Nepal in both finals. Meanwhile a professional league, matches on TV and coaching for foreign players are pushing the game onto the world map, the same way the [[@kabaddi-league|kabaddi league]] did for kabaddi.

It has a standard court, timed turns, referees and a points system. Rules were first written down in Pune in the early 1900s, and international matches now follow a rulebook used in dozens of countries.

sec.t:
A kho-kho court has a central lane with eight players crouching in a row, facing alternate directions. One more chaser is active. The defending team sends runners in, usually three at a time, who dodge and weave around the crouching line.

The active chaser can't turn back or cut across the lane. To change direction, they tap a crouching teammate and shout "kho". That player springs up and becomes the new chaser. A good team passes the chase back and forth like a relay, closing in from both sides, which is why [[@kho-kho|kho-kho]] coaches drill passing as much as running.

Runners score for their team by lasting longer. Chasers score by tagging them out. It is all about short bursts of speed, sudden stops and reading the other player, the kind of split-second thinking studied in [[@sport-science-reaction-time|reaction time]].

For decades, kho-kho stayed a school sport in India, with national championships but little money. Then, in 2022, a league called Ultimate Kho Kho started, with city teams, TV coverage and faster rules made for television. Matches got shorter, and the action became easier to follow on screen.

The World Cup was the next step. Some countries put teams together from Indian families living abroad, but many players were new to the sport. Nepal's teams were strong enough to reach both finals. Coaches in places like Kenya and Brazil liked that kho-kho needs no expensive kit, just a flat ground, two poles and some lines.

The big dream for kho-kho fans is to see it at the Asian Games and, some day, the Olympics. For that, a sport has to be played widely across many continents, with strong national federations. Kho-kho isn't there yet, but the 2025 World Cup was a big jump.

There is also a simple reason it travels well. Every child in every country already knows how to play tag, whether they call it tag, tig, chor-police or something else. Kho-kho just adds a team, a line and one shouted word. That idea, that an old village game can turn into a global sport, is exactly what happened to the pole sport of [[@sport-mallakhamb|mallakhamb]] too.

text: Before 1968, top high jumpers went over the bar facing it, rolling their body over the top. Dick Fosbury, a student from Oregon in the USA, did something odd. He ran in on a curve, turned his back to the bar, arched over it head first and landed on his shoulders.

At the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City, he won gold with a jump of 2.24 metres, an Olympic record. Within about ten years, most of the world's best jumpers had copied him. Today, almost every high jumper on Earth uses the Fosbury Flop.

Fosbury found it by trial and error as a teenager, because he couldn't master the older styles. Scientists explained why it works only later.

sec.t:
Fosbury wasn't good at the popular style of the time, called the straddle, in which you roll over the bar belly down. So in high school he went back to an older, simpler scissors style and kept fiddling with it. Each time the bar went up, he leaned back a little more. Eventually he was going over flat on his back.

In 1964 his local newspaper in Medford, Oregon, ran the headline "Fosbury Flops Over Bar". The name stuck.

Every object has a balance point called its [[centre-of-mass|centre of mass]]. For a person standing up, it's somewhere around the belly button. To get over a bar, the jumper's whole body must clear it, but their centre of mass doesn't have to.

When a flopper arches like a rainbow over the bar, their head and arms drop down on one side while their legs hang on the other. At that moment, the centre of mass can sit a few centimetres below the bar. The jumper doesn't need to lift their body's balance point as high as the bar itself, so the same leg [[@muscles|muscles]] can clear a higher bar.

The curved run-up helps too. Running in an arc makes the jumper lean in, like a cyclist on a bend, and the lean turns into a twist that rotates them back-first over the bar.

Before the flop, jumpers tried many styles. In the scissors, you swing one leg over the bar and then the other, staying almost upright. In the Western roll, popular in the early 1900s, you go over sideways. The straddle, rolling over face down, was used to set world records in the 1960s and 1970s. Each new style brought the body's middle closer to the bar, and the flop took that idea furthest of all.

The men's world record is 2.45 metres, set by Javier Sotomayor of Cuba in 1993, as of 2026. A standard doorway is only about 2 metres high. He was about 1.95 m tall, so he cleared half a metre above his own head. The women's world record is 2.10 metres, set by Yaroslava Mahuchikh of Ukraine in Paris in 2024. It broke a record that had stood for 37 years.

At the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, Mutaz Essa Barshim of Qatar and Gianmarco Tamberi of Italy were tied after hours of jumping. Barshim asked an official whether they could share gold. They could, and they did, with a hug the world remembered.

And the strangest part? Another field event had the opposite problem. Throwers got so good that officials had to change the [[@sport-science-javelin|javelin]] itself to stop it flying out of stadiums.

sec.t:
हर कॉक्लिया में बस लगभग 15,000 रोएँदार कोशिकाएँ होती हैं, और इंसानों में एक बार खराब होने पर ये दोबारा नहीं उगतीं। बहुत तेज़ आवाज़ें, या लंबे समय तक तेज़ संगीत, इन्हें नुकसान पहुँचा सकता है। शोर से आया बहरापन हमेशा के लिए रहता है, पर इससे बचा जा सकता है।

इसीलिए विश्व स्वास्थ्य संगठन सलाह देता है कि [[@sound-recording|हेडफ़ोन]] की आवाज़ धीमी रखो, बीच-बीच में ब्रेक लो, और बहुत शोर वाले कार्यक्रमों में [[@how-noise-cancel-ears|कानों की सुरक्षा]] इस्तेमाल करो। शादी के बैंड या पटाखों जैसी किसी तेज़ आवाज़ के बाद कान बजने लगें, तो समझो यह चेतावनी है।

संगीतकार लुडविग वान [[@beethoven|बीथोवन]] की सुनने की ताकत बीस-पच्चीस की उम्र में ही जाने लगी थी। ज़िंदगी के आखिर तक वे लगभग पूरी तरह बहरे हो गए, फिर भी वे संगीत लिखते रहे। वे उसे अपने दिमाग में सुनते थे।

आज [[@hearing-aids|कान की मशीनें]] आवाज़ को तेज़ करती हैं, और कॉक्लियर इम्प्लांट सीधे सुनने वाली नस तक संदेश भेज सकते हैं। बहुत-से बधिर लोग सांकेतिक भाषा इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जो अपने व्याकरण वाली एक पूरी भाषा है। भारतीय सांकेतिक भाषा और अमेरिकी सांकेतिक भाषा एक-दूसरे से उतनी ही अलग हैं जितनी हिंदी और अंग्रेज़ी।

कॉक्लिया के पास तीन घुमावदार नलियाँ होती हैं, जो एक-दूसरे से समकोण पर लगी हैं और द्रव से भरी हैं। ये महसूस करती हैं कि तुम्हारा सिर कब घूमा, झुका या हिला। पास की दो छोटी थैलियाँ [[gravity|गुरुत्वाकर्षण]] को और यह भाँपती हैं कि तुम्हारी रफ़्तार बढ़ रही है या नहीं।

दिमाग इन संदेशों को आँखों और मांसपेशियों से मिली जानकारी के साथ जोड़ता है। जब ये आपस में मेल नहीं खाते, जैसे चलती कार में किताब पढ़ते समय, तो कुछ लोगों का जी मिचलाने लगता है।

हर बीच वाले कान से गले के पिछले हिस्से तक एक पतली नली जाती है। यह कान के पर्दे के दोनों तरफ़ हवा का दबाव बराबर रखती है। जब हवाई जहाज़ ऊपर उठता है या कार घुमावदार सड़क पर किसी हिल स्टेशन की ओर चढ़ती है, तो दबाव तेज़ी से बदलता है। निगलने या जम्हाई लेने से यह नली खुलती है, और दबाव बराबर होते ही कानों में "चट" की आवाज़ होती है।

text: चेचक एक [[virus|वायरस]] से होने वाली बीमारी थी। यह एक इंसान से दूसरे में फैलती थी, तेज़ [[@fever|बुख़ार]] लाती थी और पूरे शरीर को दर्द भरे फफोलों से ढक देती थी। इसके सबसे आम रूप से बीमार पड़ने वाले हर दस में से लगभग तीन लोगों की मौत हो जाती थी। बचने वालों में से बहुतों के चेहरे पर दाग़ रह जाते थे या उनकी आँखों की रोशनी चली जाती थी।

sec.t:
चेचक बहुत पुरानी बीमारी है। मिस्र के फ़राओ रामसेस पंचम की [[mummy|ममी]] पर जो दाग़ हैं, वे शायद इसी से पड़े थे। भारत में बहुत-से समुदाय शीतला माता की पूजा करते थे, जिन्हें चेचक से जोड़ा जाता था, और उनसे रक्षा की प्रार्थना करते थे।

लोगों ने यह भी देखा कि जो चेचक से बच निकलता, उसे यह दोबारा कभी नहीं होती। इसलिए भारत, चीन, अफ़्रीका और उस्मानी साम्राज्य के कुछ हिस्सों में वैद्य-हकीम चेचक के फफोले का पदार्थ सेहतमंद लोगों की त्वचा पर खरोंचकर लगा देते थे। इसे वेरियोलेशन कहते थे। इससे आमतौर पर हल्की बीमारी होती थी, पर हमेशा नहीं।

1721 में अमेरिका के बोस्टन शहर में फैली एक [[epidemic|महामारी]] के दौरान ओनेसिमस नाम के एक अफ़्रीकी गुलाम ने पादरी कॉटन मैदर को बताया कि अफ़्रीका में यह कैसे किया जाता है। मैदर ने इस पर ज़ोर दिया, और इससे बहुत-सी जानें बचीं।

इंग्लैंड में कहा जाता था कि जिन ग्वालिनों को गायों से काउपॉक्स नाम की हल्की बीमारी हो जाती है, उन्हें चेचक नहीं होती। 1796 में एडवर्ड जेनर नाम के डॉक्टर ने इसे परखा। उन्होंने आठ साल के लड़के जेम्स फ़िप्स की बाँह पर एक छोटे-से कट में काउपॉक्स डाल दिया। बाद में उन्होंने जेम्स को चेचक के संपर्क में लाया, और लड़का बीमार नहीं पड़ा।

जेनर का तरीका वेरियोलेशन से कहीं ज़्यादा सुरक्षित था। उन्होंने इसे वैक्सीनेशन कहा, लैटिन में गाय के लिए शब्द *वक्का* से। शुरू में बहुत-से लोगों ने उनका मज़ाक उड़ाया। एक मशहूर कार्टून में टीका लगवाने वालों के शरीर से छोटी-छोटी गायें निकलती दिखाई गईं। फिर भी कुछ ही सालों में यह तरीका पूरे यूरोप, अमेरिका और भारत तक फैल गया। भारत में पहला टीका 1802 में बंबई में लगाया गया।

1974 में भारत में चेचक का भयानक प्रकोप फैला, ख़ासकर बिहार में। हज़ारों स्वास्थ्य कर्मियों ने घर-घर जाकर खोज की, और मामलों की ख़बर देने वालों के लिए इनाम रखे गए। भारत का आख़िरी मामला मई 1975 में आया। उसी साल कुछ महीने बाद, आज के [[@bangladesh|बांग्लादेश]] के एक द्वीप पर रहीमा बानो नाम की एक छोटी बच्ची चेचक के ज़्यादा जानलेवा रूप की आख़िरी मरीज़ बनी। वह बच गई।

आख़िरी कुदरती मामला, हल्के रूप वाला, 1977 में सोमालिया में आया। 1978 में इंग्लैंड के बर्मिंघम में एक महिला की मौत हुई, जिसे यह वायरस एक प्रयोगशाला से लगा था। तब से किसी को चेचक नहीं हुई।

इस वायरस के नमूने आज भी दो प्रयोगशालाओं में ताले में बंद रखे हैं, एक अमेरिका में और एक रूस में। वैज्ञानिक अब भी बहस करते हैं कि इन्हें नष्ट कर देना चाहिए या नहीं। इस बीच, इस कामयाबी ने एक और बीमारी, [[@polio-india|पोलियो]], के ख़िलाफ़ लड़ाई को हौसला दिया, और दिखाया कि जब पूरी दुनिया साथ मिलकर काम करे तो [[@vaccines|टीके]] क्या कर सकते हैं।

ये आवाज़ें हर समय होती रहती हैं, पर आमतौर पर तुम्हें पता नहीं चलता। ये सबसे तेज़ खाने के दो-एक घंटे बाद होती हैं, जब पेट लगभग ख़ाली होता है। तब आँतें बचा-खुचा साफ़ करने के लिए एक ज़ोरदार लहर भेजती हैं। आवाज़ सोखने के लिए अंदर लगभग कोई खाना नहीं होता, इसलिए गड़गड़ाहट गूँजती है। डॉक्टर इसे बोरबोरिग्मी कहते हैं। यह यूनानी शब्द है, जो सुनने में खुद उसी आवाज़ जैसा लगता है, जैसे हमारा "गुड़गुड़"।

sec.t:
तुम्हारी आँतों की दीवारों में मांसपेशियों की परतें होती हैं, जो बिना सोचे-समझे कसती और ढीली होती रहती हैं। इस दबाव को पेरिस्टैल्सिस कहते हैं। यही खाने को गले से पेट तक, और वहाँ से लगभग 6 मीटर लंबी छोटी आँत में पहुँचाता है।

साथ ही, आँतों में सिर्फ़ खाना नहीं होता। खाते और बोलते समय तुम हवा भी निगलते हो। बड़ी आँत के [[bacteria|बैक्टीरिया]] रेशे को तोड़ते हुए गैस बनाते हैं। यह सारी गैस और तरल खाने के साथ छलकते हुए आगे बढ़ते हैं, और यही आवाज़ करते हैं। कुछ गैस ऊपर की तरफ़ [[@burps|डकार]] बनकर निकल जाती है।

जब काम करने के लिए खाना होता है, तो पेट उसे तेज़ाब और [[enzyme|एंज़ाइमों]] के साथ मथकर गाढ़ा सूप बना देता है। फिर उसे धीरे-धीरे आँत में जाने देता है।

पेट ख़ाली होते ही एक अलग दिनचर्या शुरू हो जाती है। हर डेढ़ से दो घंटे पर सिकुड़न की एक ज़ोरदार लहर पेट से चलकर पूरी छोटी आँत तक जाती है। वैज्ञानिक इसे माइग्रेटिंग मोटर कॉम्प्लेक्स कहते हैं। यह सफ़ाई दल की तरह काम करती है और खाने के बचे टुकड़े, [[mucus|बलगम]] और बैक्टीरिया बाहर धकेलती है। यही वे लहरें हैं जो बड़ी, शर्मिंदा करने वाली गड़गड़ाहट पैदा करती हैं।

जैसे ही तुम फिर से खाते हो, सफ़ाई की लहरें रुक जाती हैं और आम [[@digestion-gut|पाचन]] शुरू हो जाता है।

{{story:digestion-gut}}

गुड़गुड़ और भूख अक्सर साथ आते हैं, और यह संयोग नहीं है। जब पेट कुछ देर ख़ाली रहता है, तो वह घ्रेलिन नाम का एक [[hormone|हॉर्मोन]] बनाता है। घ्रेलिन खून के रास्ते दिमाग़ तक जाता है और तुम्हें [[@hunger|भूख]] महसूस कराता है। मोटिलिन नाम का एक और हॉर्मोन सफ़ाई की उन लहरों को चालू करने में मदद करता है।

शरीर तुम्हारे खाने का समय भी सीख लेता है। अगर तुम हमेशा एक बजे दोपहर का खाना खाते हो, तो आँतें उससे थोड़ा पहले ही तैयारी शुरू कर देती हैं। पकते खाने की खुशबू भर से पेट तेज़ाब बनाने और हिलने-डुलने लगता है। इसीलिए तलते पकौड़ों की एक महक पेट में हलचल मचा देती है।

असल में नहीं, और रोकना चाहना भी नहीं चाहिए। काम करती आँतें आवाज़ करती ही हैं। तय समय पर थोड़ा-थोड़ा खाने से ज़ोरदार गुड़गुड़ कम हो सकती है। पानी पीने से थोड़ी मदद मिल सकती है। फ़िज़ी ड्रिंक गटकने या बहुत जल्दी-जल्दी खाने से गैस और बढ़ती है।

[[@sound-travel|आवाज़]] पानी और नरम ऊतकों में अच्छी तरह चलती है, और तुम्हारा पेट इन दोनों से भरा है। सन्नाटे वाले परीक्षा हॉल में एक गुड़गुड़ तुम्हें ढोल जितनी तेज़ लग सकती है, जबकि बगल वाले को शायद पता भी न चले।

डॉक्टर कभी-कभी मरीज़ के पेट पर स्टेथोस्कोप लगाकर सुनते हैं। आम गुड़गुड़ अच्छा संकेत है कि आँतें चल रही हैं। बहुत कम आवाज़ें, या दर्द के साथ बहुत तेज़ आवाज़ें, किसी गड़बड़ का सुराग दे सकती हैं।

अगर किसी के पेट में बहुत दर्द हो, सूजन हो या उल्टियाँ हों, तो किसी भरोसेमंद बड़े को बताना और डॉक्टर को दिखाना चाहिए। अकेली गुड़गुड़, हालाँकि, बस तुम्हारी आँतों का अपना काम करना है।

जानवरों के पेट भी गुड़गुड़ाते हैं। पशु डॉक्टर गाय की बाईं तरफ़ कान लगाकर सुनते हैं, जहाँ उसका बहुत बड़ा पहला पेट हर मिनट में एक-दो बार घास को मथता है। अगर वह पेट चुप हो जाए, तो डॉक्टर समझ जाते हैं कि गाय की तबीयत ठीक नहीं है।

text: In 1968, a chemist named Spencer Silver was working at 3M, a big American company that makes tapes and glues. He was trying to make a super-strong glue. Instead he made one that stuck lightly, peeled off cleanly and could be stuck down again and again.

Nobody could think of a use for it. Six years later, a colleague named Art Fry was singing in his church choir. His paper bookmarks kept slipping out of his hymn book. He remembered Silver's odd glue, and the sticky note was born.

The glue sat unused for about six years. Spencer Silver was trying to make a strong glue and ended up with a weak one. Nobody at 3M knew what to do with it until Art Fry needed a bookmark that wouldn't fall out.

sec.h: A glue made of tiny balls
sec.t:
Most glues spread out flat and grab every bit of a surface. Silver's glue was different. Under a [[microscope|microscope]] it is made of tiny sticky spheres, far smaller than a grain of sand.

Because they are round, only part of each ball touches the paper. That gives enough grip to hold a note on a wall, but not enough to tear the paper when you pull. It is a bit like holding a ball against your palm with your fingertips instead of your whole hand.

This trick depends on [[@friction|friction]] and on how closely two surfaces touch. A note sticks well to smooth paper or glass, and badly to a dusty shelf, because dust fills the gaps.

Silver called it "a solution without a problem". For years he gave talks inside 3M, hoping somebody would find a problem it could solve.

When the team made their first test notes, they needed some paper. The lab next door had a supply of scrap paper, and it happened to be canary yellow. So the first sticky notes were yellow, and yellow stuck too.

Today you can buy them in dozens of colours and shapes, from neon pink to stars and hearts. Yellow is still the classic. One reason it lasted is practical: dark ink shows up clearly on pale yellow, and a yellow square stands out on a messy desk or a grey computer screen.

In 1977, 3M tested the notes in four American cities under the name "Press 'n Peel". Hardly anyone bought them. People didn't see why they needed sticky paper.

So in 1978, 3M flooded one city, Boise in Idaho, with free samples. Once office workers tried them, about nine out of ten said they would buy more. The notes went on sale across the USA in 1980 as Post-it Notes, and reached Canada and Europe the next year. Today they are sold in well over 100 countries, including India, where students use them to mark pages in thick exam guides.

Spencer Silver lived to see his "failed" glue become one of the best-known office products ever made. He died in 2021.

Silver's glue was a [[polymer|polymer]], a substance made of long chains of [[molecule|molecules]]. Getting the balls to the right size took real chemistry. But the success came from people noticing a use that nobody had planned.

Plenty of famous inventions began this way. [[@inventions-accidents|Accidents]] gave us a purple dye, [[@accident-pacemaker|a heart pacemaker]] and a famous explosive. And Silver's story has a cousin: [[@accident-superglue|superglue]] was first thrown aside for being far too sticky.

text: A computer chip is a thin slice of silicon covered with billions of tiny electric switches called [[transistor|transistors]], all connected by metal wires thinner than many viruses. Each transistor can be on or off, which lets the chip [[@zero-to-computers|work with 1s and 0s]].

Making one is a long chain of steps. Sand is turned into ultra-pure silicon. The silicon is grown into a large crystal, sliced into thin discs called wafers, then patterned with light and chemicals hundreds of times, layer by layer. Finally the wafer is cut into individual chips, tested and sealed in a plastic or ceramic case. The whole process often takes around three months.

options.t: By shining light through a stencil onto the chip
By a robot with a very thin pen
By carving each one with a tiny knife

st.reveal: Chipmakers coat the silicon with a chemical that changes when light hits it, then shine light through a patterned mask, a bit like a stencil. The newest machines use a special kind of ultraviolet light so the lines can be extremely thin.

myth: Computer chips are made of silicone, the rubbery stuff in kitchen spatulas.
Chips are made of silicon, a hard, shiny grey element found in sand. Silicone is a different, rubbery material that contains silicon mixed with other elements. The names are easy to mix up.

sec.t:
Silicon is the second most common [[element|element]] in [[@earth-layers-crust|Earth's crust]], after oxygen. Most beach and [[@deserts-sand|desert sand]] is quartz, which is silicon joined to oxygen. Chipmakers start with very pure quartz, then heat and treat it to remove almost everything else.

The silicon must be about 99.9999999 percent pure. That is roughly one stray [[atom|atom]] in a billion. It is melted, and a small seed crystal is dipped in and slowly pulled up while turning. Silicon freezes onto it in one perfect crystal, a shining grey cylinder that can be taller than a ten-year-old.

Diamond saws slice the crystal into wafers less than a millimetre thick, usually 300 mm across. They are polished until they shine like mirrors.

{{story:glass-made}}

The patterns on a chip are far too small to draw by hand. Instead, the wafer is coated with a light-sensitive chemical. Light shines through a mask, a glass plate carrying the pattern, and the chemical changes where the light lands. The changed areas are washed away, and the uncovered silicon can then be etched or treated.

This is repeated dozens or hundreds of times to build up layers of transistors and wiring. The newest machines, made by the Dutch company ASML, use extreme [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light and cost well over a hundred million dollars each. Some of the lines they print are only a few dozen atoms wide.

A single speck of dust is like a boulder on a chip's tiny streets. So chips are made in cleanrooms, where air is filtered and pushed down from the ceiling all the time. Workers wear full-body suits, nicknamed bunny suits, with hoods, masks and boots.

Even so, not every chip on a wafer works. Each one is tested. The good ones are cut out and packaged. Some chips that work slightly less well are sold as cheaper, slower models.

The transistor was invented in 1947 at Bell Labs in New Jersey by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley. It replaced bulky glass [[vacuum|vacuum]] tubes and won them the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

In 1958 Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments built the first integrated [[circuit|circuit]], putting several parts onto one piece of material. Robert Noyce soon made a version on silicon that was easier to mass-produce. The area south of [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]] filled with chip companies and became known as [[@silicon-valley|Silicon Valley]].

Today Taiwan makes most of the world's most advanced chips. India is building its [[@semiconductors-india|first big chip factories]], including one in Dholera, Gujarat. A modern phone chip, built on the same ideas as those early [[@computers-how|computers]], holds more than 10 billion transistors.

text: Many everyday things began in India. The biggest is the way we write numbers: ten digits, 0 to 9, where a digit's place tells you its value. That system, with [[@zero-invent|zero]] as a real number, was worked out by Indian mathematicians and carried west by Arab scholars.

India also gave the world cotton cloth, an early form of chess, crystal sugar, the board game we call snakes and ladders, and some of the earliest written guides to surgery. [[@inventions-india-modern|In modern times, Indian inventors]] have built [[@prosthetics|cheap artificial legs]], helped invent fibre optics and created a way to send money by phone that the rest of the world now studies.

st.reveal: It comes from chāmpo, meaning press or knead. In 1814, Sake Dean Mahomed, a traveller from Patna, opened bathhouses in Brighton, England, offering an Indian head massage he called shampooing. The word stuck, though it later came to mean washing hair.

n.certNote: The Indian origin of our place-value digits is well established. Some other claims are less certain. Chess most likely began in India, but a few historians argue for Persia, and the meaning of some very old objects is still debated.

sec.t:
[[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] have found traces of cotton thread in the Indus region from over 5,000 years ago. Greek writers who came to India were amazed by a "wool" that grew on trees. For centuries, Indian cloth such as Dhaka muslin was so fine and so prized that it was traded across Asia, Africa and Europe.

By around the Gupta period, Indians had also learned to boil sugarcane juice until it formed crystals. The Sanskrit word khanda, meaning a piece of sugar, is probably where the English word "[[@candy-history|candy]]" comes from.

Two [[@board-games|board games]] also started here. [[@chess-india|Chaturanga]], a battle game with elephants, [[@wheel-to-chariot|chariots]], horses and foot soldiers, most likely grew into [[@pop-chess-pieces|chess]]. Gyan chaupar, a game about good and bad deeds, became [[@snakes-ladders|snakes and ladders]] once it reached Britain.

Indian metalworkers were famous too. From at least around 2,000 years ago, smiths in southern India made a very hard steel called wootz, sealed in small clay pots and heated for hours. Traders carried it to the Middle East, where it was forged into the patterned "Damascus" swords that later impressed European travellers. Modern scientists have studied wootz blades and found tiny structures inside that help explain their strength.

{{story:indus-cities}}

The ancient physician [[@sushruta|Sushruta]] is known for a Sanskrit text that describes many surgical tools and operations. One of them is a way of rebuilding a damaged nose using a flap of skin from the cheek. Doctors still recognise it as an early form of plastic surgery.

A modern example comes from [[@jaipur|Jaipur]]. In 1969, Dr P. K. Sethi and a craftsman named Ram Chandra Sharma designed a rubber artificial foot that was cheap, waterproof and flexible enough to squat, sit cross-legged and walk barefoot. The Jaipur foot has since been fitted for well over a million people around the world, often free of charge.

Narinder Singh Kapany was born in Moga, [[@punjab|Punjab]], in 1926. In the 1950s, working in London and later the United States, he did important early experiments on sending light along thin glass fibres. In 1960 he wrote an article that made the term "fibre optics" popular. Today, glass fibres carry most of the [[@internet-how|internet]]'s data across oceans and cities.

Ajay Bhatt, who grew up in India and later worked at the American company Intel, was one of the team who designed the USB plug used to connect devices.

In 2016, India launched the Unified Payments Interface, or [[@upi-payments|UPI]]. It lets anyone with a bank account and a phone send money instantly by scanning a QR code. A chaiwala on a Pune street corner can take payments as easily as a big shop. Several countries have since signed agreements to use or link with it.

text: The electric telegraph sent messages along wires as bursts of [[@electricity-made|electricity]]. Pressing a key at one end completed a [[circuit|circuit]], and a pulse of electric current raced down the wire. At the other end, a machine clicked or made a mark. Short pulses were dots, longer ones were dashes, and patterns of dots and dashes stood for letters. This was [[@codes-morse|Morse code]].

To cross oceans, engineers laid insulated [[@undersea-internet|cables along the sea floor]]. The current travelled through a copper core, protected from seawater by layers of gutta-percha, tarred cloth and iron wire. Messages that once took weeks by ship could arrive in minutes.

st.reveal: The first cable was weak, and signals came through so faintly that operators had to send each letter slowly and repeat parts. It still beat a ship, which took more than a week. The cable failed within a month.
